outputs.L1:
LAKE WALES, Florida (CNN) — Does jumping out of a plane demonstrate love? For one Florida family, it does.

Trevor Muir, 23; Darcy Shepard, 18; Harriett Shepard, 94; and Dave Shepard, 74, were ready to take the leap. Last Saturday, four generations of Darcy Shepard’s family went skydiving to celebrate her 18th birthday. The oldest jumper was Shepard’s 94-year-old great-grandmother, Harriett Shepard.

Skydiving is becoming something of a Shepard family rite of passage. Two family members had jumped before, including the family matriarch, Harriett. Three years earlier, at age 91, Harriett Shepard went skydiving because she wanted to know what it felt like. She has since become an inspiration to her great-granddaughter.

“If she can do it at 91, then I could, too,” Darcy said, explaining that she had not been allowed to jump three years ago because she had not yet turned 18.

As Darcy planned the adventure, her brother, cousins, father and grandfather decided to join her. Initially, the family invited 94-year-old Harriett to watch everyone skydive in central Florida. But Harriett, known to the family as “Honeynun,” had no interest in simply watching. She wanted to jump.

Adventure is nothing new for this family. In the past, they have gone scuba diving and hang gliding together. This time, those jumping from the plane included Harriett; Darcy; Harriett’s 74-year-old son, Dave; Dave’s 45-year-old son, Dallas, who is Darcy’s father; two cousins; a girlfriend; and a future father-in-law.

As she suited up, Harriett said she found it “exciting to be doing this with the family.”

The eight uncertified skydivers were trained and paired with tandem instructors at the Florida Skydiving Center at Lake Wales Airport. The center required Harriett to receive medical clearance from a doctor before jumping. According to Florida Skydiving, Harriett Shepard is the oldest person ever to jump at the center.

As jump time approached, Harriett remained fearless.

“I’m never scared up there,” she said. “My husband and I had a plane. I’m never afraid.”

Great-grandson Trevor Muir, another of the jumpers, said he has water-skied, jumped on a trampoline and climbed giant tree forts with his great-grandmother.

“So what’s skydiving? Just another notch in the pole,” said Trevor, 23. “We’ve done a lot of crazy things.”

The plane, a DeHavilland Twin Otter, carried the group to an altitude of 14,000 feet. The rear door opened. Pilot Eric Weaver announced over the radio: “Attention any traffic in the Lake Wales area. There will be skydiving over the Lake Wales Airport.”

The first to jump was 94-year-old Harriett, accompanied by her instructor, David “Pip” Perry. The skydivers free-fell at speeds between 120 and 150 mph before deploying their parachutes.

“Honeynun” drifted slowly toward the ground, wearing her cozy buckle-up sandals, which she finds more comfortable than closed-toe shoes. After landing, Harriett — who has battled skin cancer — appeared more fearful of the sun than of jumping from the plane.

One skydiver after another landed safely, greeted by cheers from anxious family members waiting on the ground. Eighteen-year-old Darcy was welcomed with a chorus of “Happy Birthday.” There were high-fives, family photos and exclamations of “awesome.”

Darcy hugged her great-grandmother and exclaimed, “Yay, Honeynun.”

Darcy’s father, Dallas Shepard, called it “an incredible jump that was a lot of fun.” He said skydiving with his grandmother was “kind of neat, just being able to do it with her — but she is living life, and that’s the best part.”

His father, Dave Shepard, said it was an experience he would remember for a long time.

“It was something special, where we had four generations,” he said.

Harriett Shepard admitted that her late husband would not have been pleased.

“He would have never let me do this,” she said. “He took care of me — that’s why I’m this old.”

Yet Harriett, who has lived a long and full life as an author, photographer and architect, is concerned about the publicity.

“She’s worried,” Dave Shepard said of his mother, “that the only thing people will remember her for is jumping out of an airplane.”

LAKE WALES, Florida (CNN) — Can parachuting from an airplane be a way to express affection? For one Florida family, the answer is yes.

Trevor Muir, 23; Darcy Shepard, 18; Harriett Shepard, 94; and Dave Shepard, 74, were among the relatives preparing to make the leap. Last Saturday, four generations of Darcy Shepard’s family celebrated her 18th birthday by going skydiving together. The oldest participant was Darcy’s great-grandmother, 94-year-old Harriett Shepard.

Skydiving is turning into something of a family milestone for the Shepards. Two relatives had already tried it before, including Harriett, the family matriarch. She made her first jump three years earlier, when she was 91, simply because she was curious about the experience.

Her earlier jump encouraged Darcy. “If she can do it at 91, then I could, too,” Darcy said, noting that she had not been permitted to jump three years ago because she was not yet 18.

When Darcy began organizing the birthday outing, her brother, cousins, father and grandfather all chose to take part. Initially, the family asked 94-year-old Harriett—affectionately called “Honeynun” by her relatives—to come along and watch everyone skydive in central Florida. But Harriett had no interest in staying on the ground. She wanted to jump, too.

Adventure is nothing unusual for this family. They have previously gone scuba diving and hang gliding together.

Those who jumped included Harriett; Darcy; Harriett’s 74-year-old son, Dave; Dave’s 45-year-old son, Dallas, who is Darcy’s father; two cousins; a girlfriend; and a future father-in-law. While putting on her gear, Harriett said it was “exciting to be doing this with the family.”

Because none of the eight skydivers were certified, they received training and were matched with tandem instructors at Florida Skydiving Center at the Lake Wales Airport. The center also required Harriett to get medical approval from a doctor before she could participate. According to Florida Skydiving, Harriett Shepard is the oldest person ever to jump at that center.

As the time to leap approached, Harriett showed no fear. “I’m never scared up there,” she said. “My husband and I had a plane. I’m never afraid.”

Trevor Muir, her 23-year-old great-grandson and another member of the group, said he had already water-skied, bounced on a trampoline and climbed huge tree forts with his great-grandmother. “So what’s skydiving? Just another notch in the pole,” Trevor said. “We’ve done a lot of crazy things.”

The group went up in a DeHavilland Twin Otter, which carried them to 14,000 feet. When the back door opened, pilot Eric Weaver announced by radio: “Attention any traffic in the Lake Wales area. There will be skydiving over the Lake Wales Airport.”

Harriett, 94, was the first to leave the plane, jumping with her instructor, David “Pip” Perry. The skydivers fell freely at speeds of 120 to 150 mph before opening their parachutes.

“Honeynun” then drifted gently back to earth, wearing her comfortable buckle-up sandals, which she preferred over closed-toe shoes. After touching down, Harriett—who has fought skin cancer—seemed more worried about exposure to the sun than about having jumped from the aircraft.

One by one, the skydivers landed safely, cheered on by nervous relatives waiting on the ground. Darcy, now 18, was welcomed with a group singing of “Happy Birthday.” The day brought plenty of high-fives, family pictures and shouts of “awesome.”

Darcy embraced her great-grandmother and said, “Yay, Honeynun.”

Dallas Shepard, Darcy’s father, described the experience as “an incredible jump that was a lot of fun.” He said sharing the skydive with his grandmother was “kind of neat, just being able to do it with her — but she is living life, and that’s the best part.”

His father, Dave Shepard, said it was something he would remember for years. “It was something special, where we had four generations.”

Harriett admitted that her late husband would not have approved. “He would have never let me do this,” she said. “He took care of me — that’s why I’m this old.”

Still, Harriett—who has led a full life as an author, photographer and architect—had one concern: the attention the jump was receiving. Dave Shepard said his mother was worried “that the only thing people will remember her for is jumping out of an airplane.”

**94-Year-Old Matriarch Takes the Leap With Family in Lake Wales Skydiving Adventure**

**LAKE WALES, Fla. —** On a bright Saturday morning with blue skies stretching over Polk County, four generations of the Whitaker family gathered at the Lake Wales Municipal Airport for what they called “a family reunion with a little more altitude.”

At the center of it all was 94-year-old **Eleanor “Ellie” Whitaker**, a longtime Lake Wales resident, retired school secretary, great-great-grandmother, and, as of this weekend, a first-time skydiver.

Wearing a blue jumpsuit, white sneakers and a grin that never seemed to fade, Whitaker boarded a small aircraft alongside her children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren for a tandem skydive over Central Florida. The jump, organized through a local skydiving operator at the airport, fulfilled a wish she said had been “sitting quietly on the shelf” for decades.

“I’ve watched enough people do exciting things,” Whitaker said before boarding the plane. “I figured it was time I did one myself.”

Her family, equal parts nervous and thrilled, cheered as she was fitted with a harness and introduced to her tandem instructor. The jump team said Whitaker completed the required safety briefing and medical screening beforehand, and instructors took extra time reviewing the process with her and her relatives.

“She was calm from the minute she arrived,” said one instructor. “Honestly, some of the younger family members looked more nervous than she did.”

The Whitaker family’s adventure began as a casual conversation at Eleanor’s 94th birthday dinner earlier this year. When one of her grandsons joked about making a “bucket list board,” relatives were surprised when Eleanor immediately named skydiving as something she had always wanted to try.

“She didn’t say it like a joke,” said her daughter, **Marilyn Whitaker-Hayes**, 71. “She said, ‘I want to see the world from above before I’m done seeing it.’ That stopped all of us in our tracks.”

From there, the idea grew. Her grandson, **Daniel Hayes**, began calling skydiving centers. Her great-granddaughter, **Sophie**, designed matching family T-shirts reading, “Four Generations, One Big Jump.” By the week of the event, nearly two dozen relatives had traveled to Lake Wales from across Florida, Georgia and North Carolina.

Not everyone jumped. Some stayed on the ground with signs, cameras and folding chairs, watching the aircraft climb into the morning sky. But eight family members joined Eleanor in the air, including her 72-year-old son, two grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.

As the plane circled upward, Eleanor sat strapped to her instructor near the open door, looking out over a landscape dotted with lakes, citrus groves and neighborhoods. Family members said she waved once, then disappeared into the sky.

“She just went,” Daniel said. “No hesitation. No second guessing. Just Grandma Ellie doing what she said she was going to do.”

The tandem pair free-fell for less than a minute before the parachute opened, leaving Eleanor and her instructor gliding under canopy toward the landing area. From below, her family could hear her laughing as she descended.

When her feet touched the grass, cheers erupted across the field. Eleanor raised both arms in the air and announced, “That was better than bingo.”

Relatives rushed toward her, surrounding her with hugs. Several were crying. Eleanor, however, appeared more interested in whether the video had captured her exit from the plane.

“I want proof,” she said. “Some of my friends are not going to believe this.”

For the Whitakers, the jump was more than a thrill-seeking outing. Family members said Eleanor has long been the steady center of their lives — the person who hosted holiday dinners, remembered every birthday, mailed handwritten notes and taught younger generations to “show up for each other.”

Born in 1930, Eleanor moved to Lake Wales as a young woman and spent much of her life in Polk County. She raised three children, worked in local schools and remained active in church and community groups for decades. Her family describes her as practical, deeply kind and quietly adventurous.

“She’s not reckless,” Marilyn said. “She’s brave. There’s a difference. She’s been brave her whole life, through things a lot harder than jumping out of an airplane.”

Great-grandson **Marcus Reed**, 24, said the experience changed the way he thinks about aging.

“You hear people talk like life slows down and your best stories are behind you,” Reed said. “Then you watch your 94-year-old great-grandmother jump from a plane over Lake Wales, and you realize that’s not true at all.”

Skydiving staff said tandem jumps by older adults are not unheard of, though each participant is evaluated carefully and must meet safety requirements. Eleanor’s family said they consulted with her doctor and took the decision seriously before making plans.

“She told the doctor she was going skydiving, not asking permission to be old,” Daniel joked. “But yes, we did everything the right way.”

After the jump, the family celebrated with a picnic near the airport, complete with sandwiches, cupcakes and a framed photo of Eleanor in her skydiving gear. The image showed her standing in the Florida sun, shoulders back, thumbs up.

Asked whether she would do it again, Eleanor paused only briefly.

“Maybe for 95,” she said. “But next time, I want more of them to come with me.”

For now, her family says the story will become part of Whitaker family legend — retold at birthdays, reunions and holiday tables for years to come.

As the afternoon wind moved across the landing field, Eleanor sat beneath a canopy surrounded by relatives, still wearing the blue wristband from her jump. Her great-great-granddaughter climbed into her lap and asked if she had touched the clouds.

“Almost,” Eleanor told her. “But I got close enough.”

# Can jumping out of a plane prove love? For one family, it was an 18th birthday they’ll never forget

By [Your Name]

When Darcy Shepard turned 18, she could have celebrated the milestone with a party, a dinner or a carefully frosted cake topped with candles.

Instead, she stepped to the open door of an airplane — with her 94-year-old great-grandmother nearby — and jumped.

For Darcy and her family, the skydive was more than a thrill-seeking birthday stunt. It was a multigenerational declaration of trust, nerve and affection: a way of saying “I love you” at thousands of feet above the ground, with the wind roaring too loudly for anyone to hear it.

The moment brought together family members separated not by distance, but by decades. At 18, Darcy was marking the official beginning of adulthood. Her great-grandmother, at 94, was proving that adventure does not belong only to the young.

Together, they turned a birthday into a family story that will likely be retold for years.

Skydiving is often described in the language of fear — the racing pulse, the open aircraft door, the seconds before freefall. But for families who do it together, the experience can become something softer: a shared act of courage.

There is vulnerability in it. Tandem skydivers place themselves in the hands of instructors, equipment and the people cheering them on. For Darcy’s family, that vulnerability became part of the gift. The jump was not just about falling through the sky; it was about showing up for one another in an unforgettable way.

And perhaps that is why the image resonates: a teenager and her 94-year-old great-grandmother, both choosing the same wild leap, both refusing to let age define the boundaries of celebration.

In a culture where love is often measured in messages, gifts and carefully staged photos, the Shepard family found a more dramatic expression. They chose altitude. They chose adrenaline. They chose to make a memory big enough to match the occasion.

For Darcy, turning 18 meant stepping into adulthood with the support of generations around her. For her great-grandmother, the jump was a reminder that life’s boldest chapters are not reserved for any particular age.

By the time their parachutes opened, the terror of the leap had given way to something else: relief, awe and the kind of joy that can only come from doing something you once thought impossible.

Can jumping out of a plane show love?

For Darcy Shepard and her family, the answer came somewhere between the airplane door and the ground below: yes — if you do it together.
